summary.title: Rubber Duck Problem Solving
summary.one_liner: Explaining a problem in full detail, aloud or in writing to an imaginary listener, often reveals the answer before anyone else has to help.
keywords: how to ask a good question
writing a question solves your own problem
talking through code to find bug
takeaways: Writing a detailed question forces you to organize your thinking, which often surfaces the answer to your own problem.
Stack Exchange asks askers to describe the problem with enough detail and background, state why they need the answer, and show their research.
Saying the problem out loud to an inanimate object (a rubber duck) works as well as asking a person, as shown by the clevis hanger anecdote.
Vague, context-free questions that cannot be answered are closed or deleted on Stack Exchange, which is what the guidelines aim to prevent.
summary.summary: This Coding Horror blog post by Jeff Atwood explains why Stack Exchange enforces strict question-quality rules: askers should give enough detail, context, and their own research. Atwood argues that the effort of writing a thorough question teaches "Rubber Duck problem solving," and cites reader anecdotes of answering their own questions while drafting them. He then tells a story about an engineer who, asked by his boss to explain a problem to a stuffed duck out loud, solved a pipe-hanger question mid-sentence. The post is a short opinion piece with no code or technical tutorial steps.
